options.content:
### Animals on flowers

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Records** | [Global Biotic Interactions](https://www.globalbioticinteractions.org) (GloBI) at its [snapshot of 10 September 2026](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22691479) (CC0): the records of an animal pollinating or visiting the flowers of a plant that have coordinates, 1,309,430 of 2.1 million |
| **Sources** | GloBI gathers hundreds of datasets, each under its own terms. The largest here: [EuPPollNet](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14747448) (Lanuza et al. 2025, CC BY 4.0), 579,668 records; [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org) observations, 440,325 (under each observer's licence); [DoPI](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.3801) (Balfour et al. 2022), 79,634; GBIF-US bee collections, 60,036; CropPol, 32,366; Web of Life, 22,482 |
| **Groups** | By the visitor's class, order and family as GloBI matched its name. Bees are the bee families (Apidae, Halictidae, Andrenidae, Megachilidae, Colletidae, Melittidae, Stenotritidae); wasps and ants, the rest of the Hymenoptera; then hoverflies (Syrphidae), other flies, butterflies and moths, beetles, other insects, birds and bats. A name that matched something that visits no flower (a fish, a squirrel) falls outside the groups and out |
| **Names** | A visitor or a plant by its species, or its genus when the species is unknown (*Bombus sp.*). Records named only to the family or above are left out (2 %) |
| **Pairs** | A visitor and a plant seen together at least once. The charts count pairs and places, not records: a few studies counted one crop for weeks. Sunflowers alone are 27 % of the records, and the honey bee 35 %, but 2 % of the pairs |
| **Months** | 86 % of the records have a date. A date of 1 January is read as a year alone, since DoPI, CropPol and a dozen studies give every record of a year that day: its month is left empty |
| **Places** | To 0.01°, about 1 km. A study's records often share its site's coordinates |
| **Sightings** | What the Timeline counts: a visitor on a plant at one place in one month, however many records it holds |
| **Coverage** | Where people looked: 56 % of the records are from Europe and 41 % from North America. An empty place on the map has no records, not no pollinators |
| **A visit** | An animal seen on a flower, not proof that it pollinated it |
| **Built by** | `datasets/pollinators/build.sh` in [pacha-dashboards](https://github.com/ubica-ecuador/pacha-dashboards): DuckDB reads the 95 row groups of GloBI's `interactions.parquet` that hold flower visits and writes the visits in numbers and two tables of names, joined in the browser |

options.content:
**1.3 million records of animals on flowers**, from bees to bats, at 118,264 places: 13,845 visitors and 12,072 plants, in 178,611 different pairs.

- **The great generalist:** the honey bee was seen on 3,520 plants. Next comes the common eastern bumblebee (*Bombus impatiens*), on 1,434.
- **The most visited plants:** wild carrot had 1,016 different visitors and yarrow 993. The daisy family, Asteraceae, holds 27.4 % of all the pairs.
- **Same job, different birds:** 9,562 records of 204 hummingbird species, every one in the Americas, from 53° N to 43° S. In Africa and Asia, sunbirds take the job. Nectar bats split the same way: leaf-nosed bats in the Americas, fruit bats in the Old World.
- **The visits follow the summer:** north of the tropics, places with a visit peak in July and all but vanish in December and January; south of them, they dip from May to August.
- **Mind the gaps:** 97 % of the records come from Europe and North America, where people looked.

*Press play on the months above. Click a group, a plant family, a plant or a visitor and every view follows; draw an area on the map to keep what is inside.*

spec.rawSql:
-- Every row of the dataset: the map draws a point per row and filters them with the page's picks.
-- Birds and bats last, so they are drawn over the insects; the insects shuffled, so no group covers another.
SELECT latitude, longitude, visitor_group, visitor, plant, plant_family, "month", month_mid, records
FROM $visits
ORDER BY visitor_group IN ('Birds', 'Bats'), hash(link)

spec.description: Each place where an animal was recorded on a flower, coloured by the visitor's group: bees yellow, butterflies and moths purple, hoverflies orange, other flies green, wasps and ants blue, beetles red, birds cyan, bats white. Birds and bats are drawn over the insects, so a few of them show among many bees. The map follows every pick on the page; draw an area on it to keep the places inside. Hover a point for the visitor, the plant and the month.

query.rawSql:
-- Server side, once per visit: animals seen visiting or pollinating flowers, from Global Biotic Interactions
-- (GloBI, its snapshot of 10 September 2026, CC0; each source dataset under its own terms), written by
-- datasets/pollinators/build.sh. One row per place (to 0.01°), visitor (v), plant (p) and month, with the
-- records behind it: numbers only, so they reach the browser quickly; the names are in two small tables.
SELECT latitude, longitude, v, p, "month", records
FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/pollinators/visits.parquet'

-- Server side, once per visit: the visitors' numbers, names and groups.
SELECT v, visitor, visitor_group FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/pollinators/visitors.parquet'

-- Server side, once per visit: the plants' numbers, names and families.
SELECT p, plant, plant_family FROM 'http://feeds/datasets/pollinators/plants.parquet'

spec.description: The visits with their names, joined in the browser: what every panel reads.
spec.label: Visits
spec.name: visits

source.sql:
-- In the browser: the visits with their names. link numbers each visitor and plant pair, place each place,
-- so the panels can count them. month_mid is the month at the middle of its bar (January is 1.5), so a
-- window the Timeline plays, a little over a bar wide, holds one month.
SELECT c.latitude, c.longitude, n.visitor_group, n.visitor, pl.plant, pl.plant_family, c."month", c."month" + 0.5 AS month_mid, c.records,
       c.v::BIGINT * 100000 + c.p AS link,
       ((c.latitude + 90) * 100)::INTEGER * 40000 + ((c.longitude + 180) * 100)::INTEGER AS place
FROM $visitRows AS c
JOIN $visitorNames AS n USING (v)
JOIN $plantNames AS pl USING (p)
